值得閱讀的理由

  • 反思刻板偏見：藉由眼鏡與量尺的生動比喻，帶領讀者看清自身視角的盲點，理解我們是如何在不自覺中用自身標準批判他人。
  • 融合理論與生活：將愛德華·泰勒、克利福德·紀爾茲與鮑亞士等人類學大師的經典理論，巧妙連結至台灣職場敬酒文化、法國頭巾禁令及台北車站開齋節等實例。
  • 提升公民文化素養：探討「文化」作為相互交織的有機整體，協助讀者培養跨文化理解力，學會跳脫「我族中心主義」的傲慢視角。

摘要

眼鏡的比喻與文化的本質

作者從人們面對穆斯林女性配戴頭巾時的偏見切入，指出當我們脫口而出「那些人怎麼那麼奇怪」時，往往忽略了自己早已戴上特定濾鏡。作者借用配眼鏡的比喻，說明眼鏡的鏡框與鏡片相互牽動，正如文化並非孤立存在的碎片。英國人類學家愛德華·泰勒在 1871 年將文化定義為一個複雜的整體，涵蓋知識、信仰、藝術、道德、法律與習俗等所有人類習得的能力與習慣。文化不再只是少數菁英的品味，而是整個人群共有的生活方式。然而，作者也犀利指出，泰勒在其著作《原始文化》中雖然倡導文化普遍性，卻也隱含了十九世紀歐洲文明自居頂端的單一演化論框架。這就如同在台灣職場中，新員工若因宗教拒絕敬酒，往往會被視為不合群甚至遭到考績懲罰，表面上是單純的酒水紛爭，背後牽動的卻是宗教戒律、職場服從與權力結構的全面連動。

編織意義之網：行為背後的脈絡解碼

作者進一步探討，既然人人都戴著文化眼鏡，為何各社會的鏡片顏色差異如此巨大？人類學家克利福德·紀爾茲提出著名論斷，認為「人是懸掛在由他們自己編織的意義之網上的動物」。這意味著文化研究本質上是一門詮釋與解碼的學問，相同的生理動作在不同脈絡下具有完全不同的涵義，例如生理抽搐的眨眼與帶有調情意味的使眼色便截然不同。穆斯林頭巾正是最佳例證：在阿爾及利亞獨立戰爭中，它是隱藏武器的政治抵抗工具；在法國公立學校，它成為政教分離法規下的爭議焦點；在當代印尼，它是展現個人風格的時尚符號；而在台北車站大廳的開齋節聚會中，它則是移工們溫馨節慶的情感寄託。作者提醒，當我們對異文化感到不適時，應當反躬自省：究竟是對方的生活奇異，還是我們的眼鏡早已被染上了既定的色彩？

打破出廠設定：對抗我族中心主義的傲慢

作者指出，人們習慣將自身的文化偏好當成天經地義的「出廠設定」，這種以自身文化為標竿去衡量、批判其他文化的思維，在學術上被稱為我族中心主義。十九世紀歐洲社會曾狂妄地假設全人類都在攀爬同一座文明階梯，而身處前端的歐洲自然擁有制定規範的話語權。然而，現代人類學之父法蘭茲·鮑亞士終其一生致力於打破這套單一演化的劇本。鮑亞士主張，每個文化族群都有其獨特的歷史脈絡與生存價值，絕不能草率地套用他者的尺規去論斷高下與文明程度。作者以此作結，呼籲大眾唯有認清並拿下自身長年佩戴的有色眼鏡，才能真正學會尊重多元文化背後的深刻底蘊。

================================================

Seeing Muslim women wearing veils, those who consider themselves progressive will shake their heads, saying it’s "too backward and uncivilized." But Boas would pull you back and say, "Don't laugh; that’s a meaning of life grown out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Look at France’s 2004 ban on headscarves in schools, and you’ll know. The authorities sound very reasonable, saying discreet religious symbols are allowed, but obvious ones are not. The question is, what exactly is "obvious"? Tucking a cross necklace into one’s shirt is "discreet," while a headscarf covering hair is "too conspicuous"—so who gets to decide? Of course, the majority has the final say. Commercial break: A while back, the Republic of China had a policy of distributing ten thousand NT dollars to everyone, but what society really needs now is a universal distribution of civics textbooks. This isn't just our lament about social phenomena, but our expectation for education. We are committed to remaking the Republic, and there are two paths to this: institutional reform and the popularization of civic education. That’s why we launched this basic civic education series, to achieve our goal of "distributing" civics textbooks to all. This series is designed based. on the Ministry of Education's current "108 Curriculum" for Civics and Society , hoping to explain complex ideas simply and root basic civic education with you all. If you have the means and would like to support our efforts, consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us some support, or join as a member to help us go further on this path. You can also leave comments or join our Discord or Telegram groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu-Ge. When we see people who are different from us, what truly makes us feel uneasy—the difference itself, or the tinted glasses we already wear when. looking at others? Many people have the intuition that "everyone naturally has different habits, and not seeing eye-to-eye is just a natural thing, right?" But the most dangerous part of this mindset is that it shifts the blame onto something that cannot speak for itself: "difference." When we blurt out, "Why are those people so strange?" , we have secretly taken out that ruler we use to measure others. Who exactly engraved that ruler? Let’s talk about this today: one day your glasses break,. and you take them to an optician. The master says your frame is bent and the lenses are under uneven stress, causing a hairline crack on the left, and the frame is bent because you sat on them last time, causing the temple to widen by two degrees. You only wanted to replace the nose pads, but the optician tells you that no single part of these glasses exists in isolation. The word " culture" is just like such a pair of glasses, which is why when we discuss culture, we must first learn not to. look at things in isolation. When we talk about culture, we usually think of national treasures in the Palace Museum or traditional festivals like Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn, but in sociology and anthropology, the scope of culture is much broader. It refers to a whole set of practices and ideas that a group of people learn together in daily life and that they all understand. The most classic origin of this concept comes from the British anthropologist Edward Tylor in 1871. At the beginning of his book*Primitive Culture*, he provided a. definition that is still the most cited today: culture or civilization, taken in its wide ethnographic sense, is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society. Simply put, it is how a group of people understands the world, what gods they believe in, what they consider beautiful, what rules they set, and what kind of daily life they lead. Adding everything together is what we call culture. The past imagination of.

culture was limited to the upbringing and taste possessed by a few elites, but now it has expanded to the daily life of all humanity. There is no such thing as a person without culture in the world; every society has its own complete set of culture. Tylor specifically emphasized that culture is a complex whole, where religion and law interlock, clothing and physical sensations interlock, and linguistic habits and workplace systems interlock. Just like the optician said, if you randomly pull out one part, the whole. pair of glasses will wobble. However, a contradiction in thought is hidden here . Supporters would say this definition is a milestone for cultural equality, because since everyone has culture, European colonizers could no longer use the excuse that others were uncivilized or cultureless to justify aggression. But sharp minds would ask: doesn't the title of Tylor's book, *Primitive Culture*, already secretly rank human civilization from low to high with the. word "primitive" itself? While saying everyone has culture, he still couldn't escape the self-righteous 19 th-century European evolutionary framework deep down. To give a relatable example: at a company event, a boss raises a glass and asks everyone to toast. A new employee refuses due to their faith and is immediately criticized for being unsociable and disrespectful. In their year-end review, they are even noted as needing improvement in team integration . On the surface, this seems like just. a dispute over alcohol, but if you break it down, religious precepts, Taiwan's unique workplace toasting culture, the boss's face and authority, and the power of year-end performance reviews are all locked together. You might think you’ve just declined a drink, but in reality, you are shaking the manager’s entire definition of— and authority over—conformity. In Taiwan, this cultural "fit" isn't quite fitting at all. With many Indonesian migrant workers supporting our families , headscarves have long since appeared naturally in parks, on subway cars, in. hospital corridors, and even within our own homes. But the next question immediately arises: since everyone is wearing glasses, why are the lens tints so different from one society to the next? Since every place has its own culture, where do those differences that make us feel uncomfortable or like strangers to one another actually come from? Think about the experience of getting glasses: an optometrist swaps. lenses back and forth, asking, "Is it clearer this way, or this way?" The lighting hasn't changed, and the eye chart on the wall hasn't moved, but every time the lens is changed, the world you see looks different. This is cultural difference; the external world hasn't changed, but the glass through which we view it has. Different groups of people, shaped by their unique environments, histories, and survival conditions, have each honed a way of seeing the world, but we often view these differences too rigidly—they eat with their hands, we use chopsticks. ; they touch cheeks, we shake hands. Anthropologist Clifford Geertz reminds us that this kind of understanding misses the most fascinating parts. He famously said, "Man is an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun." This means no one lives simply in a pile of rigid customs ; everyone lives in meaning, and you must place a small action back into the actor’s own context to understand it. Therefore, he argues that studying culture is like decoding—you have to look past the surface; the difference.

is not in the act itself, but in the meaning behind it. He gave an interesting example: winking and blinking. Looking only at the muscle twitch, the two are identical, but one is a flirtatious signal, while the other is just a twitch—the difference lies in the lens of the observer. Take the Muslim headscarf as an example; placing it in different contexts makes it an entirely different thing. During the Algerian War of Independence, it was a tool of political resistance, with female fighters hiding weapons. beneath their veils. In French public schools, it is legally labeled as a religious symbol, turning it into a battlefield for secularism. In contemporary Indonesian cities, it blends with fashion trends to become an accessory for young women to express their style. And during the Eid al-Fitr celebrations at the Taipei Main Station lobby, it is a warm and lively symbol of festive gathering for migrant workers. Next time you feel uncomfortable observing the behavior of a different ethnic group, why not ask. yourself: is their life actually strange, or have the lenses in our eyes long been tinted a specific color? And who helped us tint them? Who exactly fitted these lenses for us? Actually, it’s a factory setting. You spend years wearing glasses with yellowish lenses, until one day you take them off to look at a white wall and realize, " Wow, the wall is actually this white!" But before taking them off, if someone came up and told you the wall was pure. white, you might think they were crazy, because in your field of vision, that pale yellow is simply the color a wall is supposed to be. If a ruler has been placed before our eyes since birth, how on earth are we supposed to notice it? Using one's own cultural habits to measure others, only to find them increasingly strange, is academically called ethnocentrism. What’s most intriguing isn't that this phenomenon is everywhere, but why this ruler seems so self-evident and natural. 19. th-century Europe gave a very arrogant answer, believing that all human cultures were climbing the same ladder, just at different speeds. Since there was only this single path for the whole world, European civilization, being at the front, felt perfectly justified in using its own standards as the benchmark. The father of modern anthropology, Boas, spent his life overturning this arrogant script. In " Race, Language, and Culture," he argued that every cultural group has its own. unique historical context, and it is impossible to force any nation’s experience onto a single evolutionary chart. In other words, there is no shared ladder in the world; every society follows its own path. This position is called "historical particularism." He shattered the prejudices of the 19th century. Boas pointed out that culture is infinitely complex, and there is no such thing as a universal law of evolution that applies everywhere. Once you admit there is no shared, hierarchical ladder. , using your own standards to rank others becomes completely indefensible. What is the difference between these two ways of thinking? For the most direct example: seeing a Muslim woman wearing a veil, those who think they are ahead will shake their heads and say, "That’s too backward, not yet enlightened." But Boas would hold you back and say, "Don't laugh; that is a meaning of life that grew out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Take France’s 2004 school headscarf ban as.

an example. Officials spoke nicely, saying "discreet" religious symbols were allowed but "conspicuous" ones were not. The question is: what counts as conspicuous? A cross necklace tucked under a shirt is called "discreet," but a headscarf covering hair is called " too ostentatious." Who gets to make that call? The majority, of course. Ironically, the authorities claim they are protecting girls from tradition, yet if a girl speaks up to say her headscarf is her own choice, the system. simply assumes she’s been brainwashed . This is the most terrifying form of ethnocentrism; it’s never about shouting insults, but rather that arrogant certainty that "I'm doing this for your own good." Bringing the scene back to Taiwan, our schools were actually exactly the same. In the past, schools mandated short hair for all students in the name of "neatness." If a student couldn't cut their hair due to religion, parents had to write letters and go around bowing their heads to justify their "special" status . Standards are always set by the majority, leaving only the "different" individuals to sweat and struggle to explain to the whole world why they aren't "normal." Returning to those pale yellow glasses: we don't need to rush to deny our own biases. The first step is simply to admit them. The lenses in front of our eyes come with factory settings from birth. The biggest problem is that these glasses don't just color the world; they also flatten the people walking toward us into two-dimensional silhouettes. Ethnocentrism makes it harder to see the real person in front of us. When a. group of people is reduced to flat outlines in our eyes, how easily is their right to speak stripped away? Our brains are lazy and often imagine someone to be a completely different species from us, erasing their unique personalities and replacing them with rigid labels. In sociology, this is called "othering." In his classic work* Orientalism*, Edward Said argued that the West's massive theories depicting the East were never just sketches; they. were a means of establishing authority. The issue isn't whether the outsider's portrait is accurate, but rather who is holding the brush. This insight hits the blind spot: the point of criticism isn't to catch what was said wrong, but to recognize that the rules of this script are held by a select few. The people being depicted are forced to play bit parts in others 'stories forever; even if they want to rewrite the script, the microphone is never in their hands. Applying this logic back. to the Muslim headscarf: when mainstream society defines it as a symbol of female oppression, the women who wear it are left with only two roles: victims needing "civilized" salvation, or fanatics to be strictly guarded against. If they say "this is my own decision" or "this is my personal freedom," how will others perceive them? I think most people would say they've been brainwashed too deeply and haven't truly awakened; only when they weep and accuse others of persecution will everyone nod in. satisfaction and say, "See? I knew it." When a person is only allowed to be a victim or a fanatic, every word they say will be twisted into the script others want to hear. In 1958, the story of Algerian women being forced to burn their veils in public became headline news precisely because it perfectly fit the colonizer's narrative of the barbaric being saved by the civilized. Take a common trope in our news: when a migrant worker gets a certification or an award, the headline reads, "This foreign worker is different." Think.

carefully about that phrase—behind the praise lies the assumption that other migrant workers are supposed to be inferior and have no future. Right? On the surface, it’s praise; in reality, it treats them as a mere exception. If this award-winning worker tried to talk about labor conditions, overtime pay, or vacation rights in front of a microphone, these truly important voices would likely be wiped clean, because they don't fit the script. The cruelest harm of "othering" isn't how harshly people speak to you, but the way a preconceived framework strips you of the chance to defend yourself—but it doesn't end there. Have you all seen Dragon Ball? Characters wear green scouters to analyze power levels, but some levels can't be measured; you might think the device is glitchy, but the numbers are actually forced upon you. When these " power levels" are converted into government budgets, how should we evaluate them? Ranking civilizations. from high to low, distinguishing between the civilized and the barbaric, the progressive and the backward, and insisting the lower must emulate the higher—in academia, this is called cultural hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, it’s no longer just private grumbling; it becomes a roadmap guiding how power is exercised. The most famous example is political scientist Samuel Huntington, who asserted in "The Clash of Civilizations " that after the Cold War, the most serious human conflict would no longer be the ideological struggle between. capitalism and communism, but clashes between different civilizations. The world would be reshuffled along civilizational lines, making identity the most volatile battlefield. This theory exposes a reality: cultural differences are easily exploited by politicians for their own agendas. But as anthropologist Eric Wolf asked in " Europe and the People Without History," where on earth are there so many closed-off, unrelated civilizations? These civilizations, from beginning to end, were forged by humanity through. trade, conquest, and migration; civilization is the result of dynamic collisions. Looking back at the 1958 farce in Algeria where veils were publicly burned, it was the rawest official display of cultural intolerance: the French colonial government brought in troops, set up cameras, and staged a show of "savage women." The play portrayed them being saved and liberated by French civilization, packaging their colonial rule as noble enlightenment while branding local customs as symbols of backward decay. When intolerance. reaches this level, it is no longer just personal prejudice; it becomes a political act fueled by budgets, military mobilization, and carefully staged lenses. If prejudice stays in one's head, it doesn't cost a dime, but when it becomes policy, it drains massive budgets. That is why cultural intolerance is not merely a moral issue , but a genuine struggle for power. Take an example from daily life: a certain city holds a multicultural festival, with promotional materials filled with words like "inclusion" and. "respect," yet one look at the venue layout and schedule reveals the truth. Stalls for Southeast Asian migrant workers are shoved to the outermost perimeter, next to portable toilets and trash cans, with their performances relegated to a 20-minute slot at 3 PM in the scorching sun, while the main stage is generously handed over to expensive pop bands for a full hour. Promotional materials are never stupid enough to write who is superior or inferior, but the budget sheets and floor plans do, and the schedule allocations make it perfectly clear. Cultural intolerance is rarely printed.

in slogans; it usually lies quietly within government budgets. So, how do we address this issue systematically? Article 10, Paragraph 11 of the Additional Articles of the Constitution of the Republic of China explicitly affirms multiculturalism and forbids state power from leading cultural intolerance. Implemented in real life, the Taiwan Railways Administration later officially opened a Muslim prayer room on the basement floor of Taipei Main Station, equipped with a qibla and washing facilities, becoming a pioneer. among Taiwan's transport hubs. Let’s use another example: when the Algerian War of Independence broke out in November 1954, there was an object fiercely contested from the start—the white haik worn by women. In the urban warfare of Algiers, female members once used it to smuggle bombs. After the French military caught onto their inspection techniques, the women switched to European-style clothing to pass through. The French side judged that to dismantle the local society's structure of resistance, they must. first make the women take off their veils. Please note the logic behind this judgment: they were not discussing clothing; they were discussing tactics. A piece of cloth here is no longer just clothing; it is a strategic objective. On May 13, 1958, a power seizure occurred in Algiers, and on that very same day in the city center, a public unveiling ceremony was held, hosted by the wives of high-ranking garrison officers. Women stepped forward, declaring their desire to be liberated, removing their veils and burning them, shouting, "Like French women!" Cameras. circled the area while armed soldiers maintained order. A few days later, pro-French newspapers declared on their front pages that a large number of Muslim women had taken a stand. There is a set of figures here I hope you will remember: researchers estimate the actual number of participants was between a few dozen and a few hundred, while the newspaper claimed it was several thousand. If we shift the lens to the individual, the picture changes entirely. One woman who had never even worn a veil only attended because her. brother was in French custody; she was coerced into participating in exchange for his life. Thus, this exhibition of "voluntary liberation" was conditioned by duress, where the individual and the collective exposed each other. Viewed from above, it was an awakening with impressive statistics; viewed from below, it was a person's desperate calculation in an extreme situation. This is the cruelty of othering. Within that framework, her true situation could never be voiced, because the. framework only required her action, not her reasons. Now, let’s apply the five concepts mentioned today to this scene one by one. First is culture. The French were never just dealing with a piece of cloth, but with religious norms, structures, and social networks. Precisely because it was an integrated piece of a whole, the French judged that removing this one item could affect the entire situation. This judgment was tactically accurate, and that is exactly what made it so terrifying. Second is cultural difference; that same piece of cloth. meant completely different things within the two respective systems. For the French, it was proof of backwardness; for the local society, it was a part of daily life and a resource that could be used for resistance. The two sides weren't fighting over who owned the item, but over what it signified. Third is ethnocentrism. The French line of reasoning was: because our women don't wear it, not wearing it is progressive; and because not wearing it is progressive, taking it off is liberation. This logic never departed.

from its own measuring stick, yet they felt they were speaking about universal truths the entire time. Fourth is othering. Local women were predefined as a category in need of saving, so they only needed to appear and perform that act to complete the entire script. The fifth is cultural intervention. The previous four layers combined finally evolve into an action plan: selecting a date, clearing the site, and moving in. Bringing in the military, arranging the cameras, and issuing headlines—this is the complete form of intervention. It’s not just a statement, but an executable plan. Forty-six years later, the same set of "graduations"(lenses) changed location and methodology. On December 17, 2003, the French President delivered a speech advocating for an explicit ban on wearing symbols of overt religious affiliation in public primary and secondary schools. On March 3, 2004, the Senate passed the law to take effect that September, designating it as Article L 141-5-1 in the Education Code, while clarifying which religious symbols were permissible. In. this controversy, one side argues that campus should be a shared space where students are not segregated by religious affiliation, while the other side notes this line practically falls on Muslim female students, and under the name of protection, strips them of the chance to explain their reasons. The biggest difference from 1958 is the means: 1958 used the military and cameras, while 2004 used legislative procedures, committee reports, and code articles. The means shifted from. coercion to legality, the setting from a colony to the home country, and the justification from liberation to secularism. Yet one thing remains unchanged: the person deciding what that piece of cloth means is still not the person wearing it. The 1958 lens perceived the veil as backward, while the 2004 lens perceived it as insufficiently secular. The name of the lens has changed, but the lens itself remains. The one thing we shouldn't do with this example is use it to cast blame, because both eras believed they were helping. In both cases, someone. else substituted the wearer to decide what that piece of cloth meant. Any society, while acting under the assumption of good intentions, might use its own ruler to measure everyone else. When you discover our cultures are different, what should we do? In reality, the filter cannot be taken off ; anyone viewing the world must do so through some language, some set of customs, and some span of history. This is not a defect; this is precisely the result of having a culture. So, if. someone tells you, "I am completely objective and have no stance," that statement itself is a pair of very thick, prescribed glasses. What we can actually do are three things: first, know that you are wearing them; second, recognize who etched the graduations onto those lenses. Third, before passing judgment on others' lives, let them first explain what that thing means within their own system. These three things aren't romantic, but they are all things that can be practiced. Finally, A-Niu has a question for everyone to think about: suppose a. public high school bans students from wearing religious symbols on campus, would you support it? 值得閱讀的理由

  • 反思刻板偏見：藉由眼鏡與量尺的生動比喻，帶領讀者看清自身視角的盲點，理解我們是如何在不自覺中用自身標準批判他人。
  • 融合理論與生活：將愛德華·泰勒、克利福德·紀爾茲與鮑亞士等人類學大師的經典理論，巧妙連結至台灣職場敬酒文化、法國頭巾禁令及台北車站開齋節等實例。
  • 提升公民文化素養：探討「文化」作為相互交織的有機整體，協助讀者培養跨文化理解力，學會跳脫「我族中心主義」的傲慢視角。

摘要

眼鏡的比喻與文化的本質

作者從人們面對穆斯林女性配戴頭巾時的偏見切入，指出當我們脫口而出「那些人怎麼那麼奇怪」時，往往忽略了自己早已戴上特定濾鏡。作者借用配眼鏡的比喻，說明眼鏡的鏡框與鏡片相互牽動，正如文化並非孤立存在的碎片。英國人類學家愛德華·泰勒在 1871 年將文化定義為一個複雜的整體，涵蓋知識、信仰、藝術、道德、法律與習俗等所有人類習得的能力與習慣。文化不再只是少數菁英的品味，而是整個人群共有的生活方式。然而，作者也犀利指出，泰勒在其著作《原始文化》中雖然倡導文化普遍性，卻也隱含了十九世紀歐洲文明自居頂端的單一演化論框架。這就如同在台灣職場中，新員工若因宗教拒絕敬酒，往往會被視為不合群甚至遭到考績懲罰，表面上是單純的酒水紛爭，背後牽動的卻是宗教戒律、職場服從與權力結構的全面連動。

編織意義之網：行為背後的脈絡解碼

作者進一步探討，既然人人都戴著文化眼鏡，為何各社會的鏡片顏色差異如此巨大？人類學家克利福德·紀爾茲提出著名論斷，認為「人是懸掛在由他們自己編織的意義之網上的動物」。這意味著文化研究本質上是一門詮釋與解碼的學問，相同的生理動作在不同脈絡下具有完全不同的涵義，例如生理抽搐的眨眼與帶有調情意味的使眼色便截然不同。穆斯林頭巾正是最佳例證：在阿爾及利亞獨立戰爭中，它是隱藏武器的政治抵抗工具；在法國公立學校，它成為政教分離法規下的爭議焦點；在當代印尼，它是展現個人風格的時尚符號；而在台北車站大廳的開齋節聚會中，它則是移工們溫馨節慶的情感寄託。作者提醒，當我們對異文化感到不適時，應當反躬自省：究竟是對方的生活奇異，還是我們的眼鏡早已被染上了既定的色彩？

打破出廠設定：對抗我族中心主義的傲慢

作者指出，人們習慣將自身的文化偏好當成天經地義的「出廠設定」，這種以自身文化為標竿去衡量、批判其他文化的思維，在學術上被稱為我族中心主義。十九世紀歐洲社會曾狂妄地假設全人類都在攀爬同一座文明階梯，而身處前端的歐洲自然擁有制定規範的話語權。然而，現代人類學之父法蘭茲·鮑亞士終其一生致力於打破這套單一演化的劇本。鮑亞士主張，每個文化族群都有其獨特的歷史脈絡與生存價值，絕不能草率地套用他者的尺規去論斷高下與文明程度。作者以此作結，呼籲大眾唯有認清並拿下自身長年佩戴的有色眼鏡，才能真正學會尊重多元文化背後的深刻底蘊。

================================================

Seeing Muslim women wearing veils, those who consider themselves progressive will shake their heads, saying it’s "too backward and uncivilized." But Boas would pull you back and say, "Don't laugh; that’s a meaning of life grown out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Look at France’s 2004 ban on headscarves in schools, and you’ll know. The authorities sound very reasonable, saying discreet religious symbols are allowed, but obvious ones are not. The question is, what exactly is "obvious"? Tucking a cross necklace into one’s shirt is "discreet," while a headscarf covering hair is "too conspicuous"—so who gets to decide? Of course, the majority has the final say. Commercial break: A while back, the Republic of China had a policy of distributing ten thousand NT dollars to everyone, but what society really needs now is a universal distribution of civics textbooks. This isn't just our lament about social phenomena, but our expectation for education. We are committed to remaking the Republic, and there are two paths to this: institutional reform and the popularization of civic education. That’s why we launched this basic civic education series, to achieve our goal of "distributing" civics textbooks to all. This series is designed based. on the Ministry of Education's current "108 Curriculum" for Civics and Society , hoping to explain complex ideas simply and root basic civic education with you all. If you have the means and would like to support our efforts, consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us some support, or join as a member to help us go further on this path. You can also leave comments or join our Discord or Telegram groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu-Ge. When we see people who are different from us, what truly makes us feel uneasy—the difference itself, or the tinted glasses we already wear when. looking at others? Many people have the intuition that "everyone naturally has different habits, and not seeing eye-to-eye is just a natural thing, right?" But the most dangerous part of this mindset is that it shifts the blame onto something that cannot speak for itself: "difference." When we blurt out, "Why are those people so strange?" , we have secretly taken out that ruler we use to measure others. Who exactly engraved that ruler? Let’s talk about this today: one day your glasses break,. and you take them to an optician. The master says your frame is bent and the lenses are under uneven stress, causing a hairline crack on the left, and the frame is bent because you sat on them last time, causing the temple to widen by two degrees. You only wanted to replace the nose pads, but the optician tells you that no single part of these glasses exists in isolation. The word " culture" is just like such a pair of glasses, which is why when we discuss culture, we must first learn not to. look at things in isolation. When we talk about culture, we usually think of national treasures in the Palace Museum or traditional festivals like Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn, but in sociology and anthropology, the scope of culture is much broader. It refers to a whole set of practices and ideas that a group of people learn together in daily life and that they all understand. The most classic origin of this concept comes from the British anthropologist Edward Tylor in 1871. At the beginning of his book*Primitive Culture*, he provided a. definition that is still the most cited today: culture or civilization, taken in its wide ethnographic sense, is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society. Simply put, it is how a group of people understands the world, what gods they believe in, what they consider beautiful, what rules they set, and what kind of daily life they lead. Adding everything together is what we call culture. The past imagination of.

culture was limited to the upbringing and taste possessed by a few elites, but now it has expanded to the daily life of all humanity. There is no such thing as a person without culture in the world; every society has its own complete set of culture. Tylor specifically emphasized that culture is a complex whole, where religion and law interlock, clothing and physical sensations interlock, and linguistic habits and workplace systems interlock. Just like the optician said, if you randomly pull out one part, the whole. pair of glasses will wobble. However, a contradiction in thought is hidden here . Supporters would say this definition is a milestone for cultural equality, because since everyone has culture, European colonizers could no longer use the excuse that others were uncivilized or cultureless to justify aggression. But sharp minds would ask: doesn't the title of Tylor's book, *Primitive Culture*, already secretly rank human civilization from low to high with the. word "primitive" itself? While saying everyone has culture, he still couldn't escape the self-righteous 19 th-century European evolutionary framework deep down. To give a relatable example: at a company event, a boss raises a glass and asks everyone to toast. A new employee refuses due to their faith and is immediately criticized for being unsociable and disrespectful. In their year-end review, they are even noted as needing improvement in team integration . On the surface, this seems like just. a dispute over alcohol, but if you break it down, religious precepts, Taiwan's unique workplace toasting culture, the boss's face and authority, and the power of year-end performance reviews are all locked together. You might think you’ve just declined a drink, but in reality, you are shaking the manager’s entire definition of— and authority over—conformity. In Taiwan, this cultural "fit" isn't quite fitting at all. With many Indonesian migrant workers supporting our families , headscarves have long since appeared naturally in parks, on subway cars, in. hospital corridors, and even within our own homes. But the next question immediately arises: since everyone is wearing glasses, why are the lens tints so different from one society to the next? Since every place has its own culture, where do those differences that make us feel uncomfortable or like strangers to one another actually come from? Think about the experience of getting glasses: an optometrist swaps. lenses back and forth, asking, "Is it clearer this way, or this way?" The lighting hasn't changed, and the eye chart on the wall hasn't moved, but every time the lens is changed, the world you see looks different. This is cultural difference; the external world hasn't changed, but the glass through which we view it has. Different groups of people, shaped by their unique environments, histories, and survival conditions, have each honed a way of seeing the world, but we often view these differences too rigidly—they eat with their hands, we use chopsticks. ; they touch cheeks, we shake hands. Anthropologist Clifford Geertz reminds us that this kind of understanding misses the most fascinating parts. He famously said, "Man is an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun." This means no one lives simply in a pile of rigid customs ; everyone lives in meaning, and you must place a small action back into the actor’s own context to understand it. Therefore, he argues that studying culture is like decoding—you have to look past the surface; the difference.

is not in the act itself, but in the meaning behind it. He gave an interesting example: winking and blinking. Looking only at the muscle twitch, the two are identical, but one is a flirtatious signal, while the other is just a twitch—the difference lies in the lens of the observer. Take the Muslim headscarf as an example; placing it in different contexts makes it an entirely different thing. During the Algerian War of Independence, it was a tool of political resistance, with female fighters hiding weapons. beneath their veils. In French public schools, it is legally labeled as a religious symbol, turning it into a battlefield for secularism. In contemporary Indonesian cities, it blends with fashion trends to become an accessory for young women to express their style. And during the Eid al-Fitr celebrations at the Taipei Main Station lobby, it is a warm and lively symbol of festive gathering for migrant workers. Next time you feel uncomfortable observing the behavior of a different ethnic group, why not ask. yourself: is their life actually strange, or have the lenses in our eyes long been tinted a specific color? And who helped us tint them? Who exactly fitted these lenses for us? Actually, it’s a factory setting. You spend years wearing glasses with yellowish lenses, until one day you take them off to look at a white wall and realize, " Wow, the wall is actually this white!" But before taking them off, if someone came up and told you the wall was pure. white, you might think they were crazy, because in your field of vision, that pale yellow is simply the color a wall is supposed to be. If a ruler has been placed before our eyes since birth, how on earth are we supposed to notice it? Using one's own cultural habits to measure others, only to find them increasingly strange, is academically called ethnocentrism. What’s most intriguing isn't that this phenomenon is everywhere, but why this ruler seems so self-evident and natural. 19. th-century Europe gave a very arrogant answer, believing that all human cultures were climbing the same ladder, just at different speeds. Since there was only this single path for the whole world, European civilization, being at the front, felt perfectly justified in using its own standards as the benchmark. The father of modern anthropology, Boas, spent his life overturning this arrogant script. In " Race, Language, and Culture," he argued that every cultural group has its own. unique historical context, and it is impossible to force any nation’s experience onto a single evolutionary chart. In other words, there is no shared ladder in the world; every society follows its own path. This position is called "historical particularism." He shattered the prejudices of the 19th century. Boas pointed out that culture is infinitely complex, and there is no such thing as a universal law of evolution that applies everywhere. Once you admit there is no shared, hierarchical ladder. , using your own standards to rank others becomes completely indefensible. What is the difference between these two ways of thinking? For the most direct example: seeing a Muslim woman wearing a veil, those who think they are ahead will shake their heads and say, "That’s too backward, not yet enlightened." But Boas would hold you back and say, "Don't laugh; that is a meaning of life that grew out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Take France’s 2004 school headscarf ban as.

an example. Officials spoke nicely, saying "discreet" religious symbols were allowed but "conspicuous" ones were not. The question is: what counts as conspicuous? A cross necklace tucked under a shirt is called "discreet," but a headscarf covering hair is called " too ostentatious." Who gets to make that call? The majority, of course. Ironically, the authorities claim they are protecting girls from tradition, yet if a girl speaks up to say her headscarf is her own choice, the system. simply assumes she’s been brainwashed . This is the most terrifying form of ethnocentrism; it’s never about shouting insults, but rather that arrogant certainty that "I'm doing this for your own good." Bringing the scene back to Taiwan, our schools were actually exactly the same. In the past, schools mandated short hair for all students in the name of "neatness." If a student couldn't cut their hair due to religion, parents had to write letters and go around bowing their heads to justify their "special" status . Standards are always set by the majority, leaving only the "different" individuals to sweat and struggle to explain to the whole world why they aren't "normal." Returning to those pale yellow glasses: we don't need to rush to deny our own biases. The first step is simply to admit them. The lenses in front of our eyes come with factory settings from birth. The biggest problem is that these glasses don't just color the world; they also flatten the people walking toward us into two-dimensional silhouettes. Ethnocentrism makes it harder to see the real person in front of us. When a. group of people is reduced to flat outlines in our eyes, how easily is their right to speak stripped away? Our brains are lazy and often imagine someone to be a completely different species from us, erasing their unique personalities and replacing them with rigid labels. In sociology, this is called "othering." In his classic work* Orientalism*, Edward Said argued that the West's massive theories depicting the East were never just sketches; they. were a means of establishing authority. The issue isn't whether the outsider's portrait is accurate, but rather who is holding the brush. This insight hits the blind spot: the point of criticism isn't to catch what was said wrong, but to recognize that the rules of this script are held by a select few. The people being depicted are forced to play bit parts in others 'stories forever; even if they want to rewrite the script, the microphone is never in their hands. Applying this logic back. to the Muslim headscarf: when mainstream society defines it as a symbol of female oppression, the women who wear it are left with only two roles: victims needing "civilized" salvation, or fanatics to be strictly guarded against. If they say "this is my own decision" or "this is my personal freedom," how will others perceive them? I think most people would say they've been brainwashed too deeply and haven't truly awakened; only when they weep and accuse others of persecution will everyone nod in. satisfaction and say, "See? I knew it." When a person is only allowed to be a victim or a fanatic, every word they say will be twisted into the script others want to hear. In 1958, the story of Algerian women being forced to burn their veils in public became headline news precisely because it perfectly fit the colonizer's narrative of the barbaric being saved by the civilized. Take a common trope in our news: when a migrant worker gets a certification or an award, the headline reads, "This foreign worker is different." Think.

carefully about that phrase—behind the praise lies the assumption that other migrant workers are supposed to be inferior and have no future. Right? On the surface, it’s praise; in reality, it treats them as a mere exception. If this award-winning worker tried to talk about labor conditions, overtime pay, or vacation rights in front of a microphone, these truly important voices would likely be wiped clean, because they don't fit the script. The cruelest harm of "othering" isn't how harshly people speak to you, but the way a preconceived framework strips you of the chance to defend yourself—but it doesn't end there. Have you all seen Dragon Ball? Characters wear green scouters to analyze power levels, but some levels can't be measured; you might think the device is glitchy, but the numbers are actually forced upon you. When these " power levels" are converted into government budgets, how should we evaluate them? Ranking civilizations. from high to low, distinguishing between the civilized and the barbaric, the progressive and the backward, and insisting the lower must emulate the higher—in academia, this is called cultural hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, it’s no longer just private grumbling; it becomes a roadmap guiding how power is exercised. The most famous example is political scientist Samuel Huntington, who asserted in "The Clash of Civilizations " that after the Cold War, the most serious human conflict would no longer be the ideological struggle between. capitalism and communism, but clashes between different civilizations. The world would be reshuffled along civilizational lines, making identity the most volatile battlefield. This theory exposes a reality: cultural differences are easily exploited by politicians for their own agendas. But as anthropologist Eric Wolf asked in " Europe and the People Without History," where on earth are there so many closed-off, unrelated civilizations? These civilizations, from beginning to end, were forged by humanity through. trade, conquest, and migration; civilization is the result of dynamic collisions. Looking back at the 1958 farce in Algeria where veils were publicly burned, it was the rawest official display of cultural intolerance: the French colonial government brought in troops, set up cameras, and staged a show of "savage women." The play portrayed them being saved and liberated by French civilization, packaging their colonial rule as noble enlightenment while branding local customs as symbols of backward decay. When intolerance. reaches this level, it is no longer just personal prejudice; it becomes a political act fueled by budgets, military mobilization, and carefully staged lenses. If prejudice stays in one's head, it doesn't cost a dime, but when it becomes policy, it drains massive budgets. That is why cultural intolerance is not merely a moral issue , but a genuine struggle for power. Take an example from daily life: a certain city holds a multicultural festival, with promotional materials filled with words like "inclusion" and. "respect," yet one look at the venue layout and schedule reveals the truth. Stalls for Southeast Asian migrant workers are shoved to the outermost perimeter, next to portable toilets and trash cans, with their performances relegated to a 20-minute slot at 3 PM in the scorching sun, while the main stage is generously handed over to expensive pop bands for a full hour. Promotional materials are never stupid enough to write who is superior or inferior, but the budget sheets and floor plans do, and the schedule allocations make it perfectly clear. Cultural intolerance is rarely printed.

in slogans; it usually lies quietly within government budgets. So, how do we address this issue systematically? Article 10, Paragraph 11 of the Additional Articles of the Constitution of the Republic of China explicitly affirms multiculturalism and forbids state power from leading cultural intolerance. Implemented in real life, the Taiwan Railways Administration later officially opened a Muslim prayer room on the basement floor of Taipei Main Station, equipped with a qibla and washing facilities, becoming a pioneer. among Taiwan's transport hubs. Let’s use another example: when the Algerian War of Independence broke out in November 1954, there was an object fiercely contested from the start—the white haik worn by women. In the urban warfare of Algiers, female members once used it to smuggle bombs. After the French military caught onto their inspection techniques, the women switched to European-style clothing to pass through. The French side judged that to dismantle the local society's structure of resistance, they must. first make the women take off their veils. Please note the logic behind this judgment: they were not discussing clothing; they were discussing tactics. A piece of cloth here is no longer just clothing; it is a strategic objective. On May 13, 1958, a power seizure occurred in Algiers, and on that very same day in the city center, a public unveiling ceremony was held, hosted by the wives of high-ranking garrison officers. Women stepped forward, declaring their desire to be liberated, removing their veils and burning them, shouting, "Like French women!" Cameras. circled the area while armed soldiers maintained order. A few days later, pro-French newspapers declared on their front pages that a large number of Muslim women had taken a stand. There is a set of figures here I hope you will remember: researchers estimate the actual number of participants was between a few dozen and a few hundred, while the newspaper claimed it was several thousand. If we shift the lens to the individual, the picture changes entirely. One woman who had never even worn a veil only attended because her. brother was in French custody; she was coerced into participating in exchange for his life. Thus, this exhibition of "voluntary liberation" was conditioned by duress, where the individual and the collective exposed each other. Viewed from above, it was an awakening with impressive statistics; viewed from below, it was a person's desperate calculation in an extreme situation. This is the cruelty of othering. Within that framework, her true situation could never be voiced, because the. framework only required her action, not her reasons. Now, let’s apply the five concepts mentioned today to this scene one by one. First is culture. The French were never just dealing with a piece of cloth, but with religious norms, structures, and social networks. Precisely because it was an integrated piece of a whole, the French judged that removing this one item could affect the entire situation. This judgment was tactically accurate, and that is exactly what made it so terrifying. Second is cultural difference; that same piece of cloth. meant completely different things within the two respective systems. For the French, it was proof of backwardness; for the local society, it was a part of daily life and a resource that could be used for resistance. The two sides weren't fighting over who owned the item, but over what it signified. Third is ethnocentrism. The French line of reasoning was: because our women don't wear it, not wearing it is progressive; and because not wearing it is progressive, taking it off is liberation. This logic never departed.

from its own measuring stick, yet they felt they were speaking about universal truths the entire time. Fourth is othering. Local women were predefined as a category in need of saving, so they only needed to appear and perform that act to complete the entire script. The fifth is cultural intervention. The previous four layers combined finally evolve into an action plan: selecting a date, clearing the site, and moving in. Bringing in the military, arranging the cameras, and issuing headlines—this is the complete form of intervention. It’s not just a statement, but an executable plan. Forty-six years later, the same set of "graduations"(lenses) changed location and methodology. On December 17, 2003, the French President delivered a speech advocating for an explicit ban on wearing symbols of overt religious affiliation in public primary and secondary schools. On March 3, 2004, the Senate passed the law to take effect that September, designating it as Article L 141-5-1 in the Education Code, while clarifying which religious symbols were permissible. In. this controversy, one side argues that campus should be a shared space where students are not segregated by religious affiliation, while the other side notes this line practically falls on Muslim female students, and under the name of protection, strips them of the chance to explain their reasons. The biggest difference from 1958 is the means: 1958 used the military and cameras, while 2004 used legislative procedures, committee reports, and code articles. The means shifted from. coercion to legality, the setting from a colony to the home country, and the justification from liberation to secularism. Yet one thing remains unchanged: the person deciding what that piece of cloth means is still not the person wearing it. The 1958 lens perceived the veil as backward, while the 2004 lens perceived it as insufficiently secular. The name of the lens has changed, but the lens itself remains. The one thing we shouldn't do with this example is use it to cast blame, because both eras believed they were helping. In both cases, someone. else substituted the wearer to decide what that piece of cloth meant. Any society, while acting under the assumption of good intentions, might use its own ruler to measure everyone else. When you discover our cultures are different, what should we do? In reality, the filter cannot be taken off ; anyone viewing the world must do so through some language, some set of customs, and some span of history. This is not a defect; this is precisely the result of having a culture. So, if. someone tells you, "I am completely objective and have no stance," that statement itself is a pair of very thick, prescribed glasses. What we can actually do are three things: first, know that you are wearing them; second, recognize who etched the graduations onto those lenses. Third, before passing judgment on others' lives, let them first explain what that thing means within their own system. These three things aren't romantic, but they are all things that can be practiced. Finally, A-Niu has a question for everyone to think about: suppose a. public high school bans students from wearing religious symbols on campus, would you support it? Please take a stand and explain your reasoning. We welcome you to share your thoughts. Our channel has always been committed to the ideals of self-discipline and republicanism, hoping to raise awareness of democratic values through civic education and historical consciousness. If you enjoyed this episode, don't forget to like, subscribe, and share it with others. You are also welcome to join our membership. We'll see you next time, bye.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 反思刻板偏見：藉由眼鏡與量尺的生動比喻，帶領讀者看清自身視角的盲點，理解我們是如何在不自覺中用自身標準批判他人。
  • 融合理論與生活：將愛德華·泰勒、克利福德·紀爾茲與鮑亞士等人類學大師的經典理論，巧妙連結至台灣職場敬酒文化、法國頭巾禁令及台北車站開齋節等實例。
  • 提升公民文化素養：探討「文化」作為相互交織的有機整體，協助讀者培養跨文化理解力，學會跳脫「我族中心主義」的傲慢視角。

摘要

眼鏡的比喻與文化的本質

作者從人們面對穆斯林女性配戴頭巾時的偏見切入，指出當我們脫口而出「那些人怎麼那麼奇怪」時，往往忽略了自己早已戴上特定濾鏡。作者借用配眼鏡的比喻，說明眼鏡的鏡框與鏡片相互牽動，正如文化並非孤立存在的碎片。英國人類學家愛德華·泰勒在 1871 年將文化定義為一個複雜的整體，涵蓋知識、信仰、藝術、道德、法律與習俗等所有人類習得的能力與習慣。文化不再只是少數菁英的品味，而是整個人群共有的生活方式。然而，作者也犀利指出，泰勒在其著作《原始文化》中雖然倡導文化普遍性，卻也隱含了十九世紀歐洲文明自居頂端的單一演化論框架。這就如同在台灣職場中，新員工若因宗教拒絕敬酒，往往會被視為不合群甚至遭到考績懲罰，表面上是單純的酒水紛爭，背後牽動的卻是宗教戒律、職場服從與權力結構的全面連動。

編織意義之網：行為背後的脈絡解碼

作者進一步探討，既然人人都戴著文化眼鏡，為何各社會的鏡片顏色差異如此巨大？人類學家克利福德·紀爾茲提出著名論斷，認為「人是懸掛在由他們自己編織的意義之網上的動物」。這意味著文化研究本質上是一門詮釋與解碼的學問，相同的生理動作在不同脈絡下具有完全不同的涵義，例如生理抽搐的眨眼與帶有調情意味的使眼色便截然不同。穆斯林頭巾正是最佳例證：在阿爾及利亞獨立戰爭中，它是隱藏武器的政治抵抗工具；在法國公立學校，它成為政教分離法規下的爭議焦點；在當代印尼，它是展現個人風格的時尚符號；而在台北車站大廳的開齋節聚會中，它則是移工們溫馨節慶的情感寄託。作者提醒，當我們對異文化感到不適時，應當反躬自省：究竟是對方的生活奇異，還是我們的眼鏡早已被染上了既定的色彩？

打破出廠設定：對抗我族中心主義的傲慢

作者指出，人們習慣將自身的文化偏好當成天經地義的「出廠設定」，這種以自身文化為標竿去衡量、批判其他文化的思維，在學術上被稱為我族中心主義。十九世紀歐洲社會曾狂妄地假設全人類都在攀爬同一座文明階梯，而身處前端的歐洲自然擁有制定規範的話語權。然而，現代人類學之父法蘭茲·鮑亞士終其一生致力於打破這套單一演化的劇本。鮑亞士主張，每個文化族群都有其獨特的歷史脈絡與生存價值，絕不能草率地套用他者的尺規去論斷高下與文明程度。作者以此作結，呼籲大眾唯有認清並拿下自身長年佩戴的有色眼鏡，才能真正學會尊重多元文化背後的深刻底蘊。

================================================

Seeing Muslim women wearing veils, those who consider themselves progressive will shake their heads, saying it’s "too backward and uncivilized." But Boas would pull you back and say, "Don't laugh; that’s a meaning of life grown out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Look at France’s 2004 ban on headscarves in schools, and you’ll know. The authorities sound very reasonable, saying discreet religious symbols are allowed, but obvious ones are not. The question is, what exactly is "obvious"? Tucking a cross necklace into one’s shirt is "discreet," while a headscarf covering hair is "too conspicuous"—so who gets to decide? Of course, the majority has the final say. Commercial break: A while back, the Republic of China had a policy of distributing ten thousand NT dollars to everyone, but what society really needs now is a universal distribution of civics textbooks. This isn't just our lament about social phenomena, but our expectation for education. We are committed to remaking the Republic, and there are two paths to this: institutional reform and the popularization of civic education. That’s why we launched this basic civic education series, to achieve our goal of "distributing" civics textbooks to all. This series is designed based. on the Ministry of Education's current "108 Curriculum" for Civics and Society , hoping to explain complex ideas simply and root basic civic education with you all. If you have the means and would like to support our efforts, consider clicking "Super Thanks" to give us some support, or join as a member to help us go further on this path. You can also leave comments or join our Discord or Telegram groups, and let's work together to make the future better. Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu-Ge. When we see people who are different from us, what truly makes us feel uneasy—the difference itself, or the tinted glasses we already wear when. looking at others? Many people have the intuition that "everyone naturally has different habits, and not seeing eye-to-eye is just a natural thing, right?" But the most dangerous part of this mindset is that it shifts the blame onto something that cannot speak for itself: "difference." When we blurt out, "Why are those people so strange?" , we have secretly taken out that ruler we use to measure others. Who exactly engraved that ruler? Let’s talk about this today: one day your glasses break,. and you take them to an optician. The master says your frame is bent and the lenses are under uneven stress, causing a hairline crack on the left, and the frame is bent because you sat on them last time, causing the temple to widen by two degrees. You only wanted to replace the nose pads, but the optician tells you that no single part of these glasses exists in isolation. The word " culture" is just like such a pair of glasses, which is why when we discuss culture, we must first learn not to. look at things in isolation. When we talk about culture, we usually think of national treasures in the Palace Museum or traditional festivals like Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn, but in sociology and anthropology, the scope of culture is much broader. It refers to a whole set of practices and ideas that a group of people learn together in daily life and that they all understand. The most classic origin of this concept comes from the British anthropologist Edward Tylor in 1871. At the beginning of his book*Primitive Culture*, he provided a. definition that is still the most cited today: culture or civilization, taken in its wide ethnographic sense, is that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society. Simply put, it is how a group of people understands the world, what gods they believe in, what they consider beautiful, what rules they set, and what kind of daily life they lead. Adding everything together is what we call culture. The past imagination of.

culture was limited to the upbringing and taste possessed by a few elites, but now it has expanded to the daily life of all humanity. There is no such thing as a person without culture in the world; every society has its own complete set of culture. Tylor specifically emphasized that culture is a complex whole, where religion and law interlock, clothing and physical sensations interlock, and linguistic habits and workplace systems interlock. Just like the optician said, if you randomly pull out one part, the whole. pair of glasses will wobble. However, a contradiction in thought is hidden here . Supporters would say this definition is a milestone for cultural equality, because since everyone has culture, European colonizers could no longer use the excuse that others were uncivilized or cultureless to justify aggression. But sharp minds would ask: doesn't the title of Tylor's book, *Primitive Culture*, already secretly rank human civilization from low to high with the. word "primitive" itself? While saying everyone has culture, he still couldn't escape the self-righteous 19 th-century European evolutionary framework deep down. To give a relatable example: at a company event, a boss raises a glass and asks everyone to toast. A new employee refuses due to their faith and is immediately criticized for being unsociable and disrespectful. In their year-end review, they are even noted as needing improvement in team integration . On the surface, this seems like just. a dispute over alcohol, but if you break it down, religious precepts, Taiwan's unique workplace toasting culture, the boss's face and authority, and the power of year-end performance reviews are all locked together. You might think you’ve just declined a drink, but in reality, you are shaking the manager’s entire definition of— and authority over—conformity. In Taiwan, this cultural "fit" isn't quite fitting at all. With many Indonesian migrant workers supporting our families , headscarves have long since appeared naturally in parks, on subway cars, in. hospital corridors, and even within our own homes. But the next question immediately arises: since everyone is wearing glasses, why are the lens tints so different from one society to the next? Since every place has its own culture, where do those differences that make us feel uncomfortable or like strangers to one another actually come from? Think about the experience of getting glasses: an optometrist swaps. lenses back and forth, asking, "Is it clearer this way, or this way?" The lighting hasn't changed, and the eye chart on the wall hasn't moved, but every time the lens is changed, the world you see looks different. This is cultural difference; the external world hasn't changed, but the glass through which we view it has. Different groups of people, shaped by their unique environments, histories, and survival conditions, have each honed a way of seeing the world, but we often view these differences too rigidly—they eat with their hands, we use chopsticks. ; they touch cheeks, we shake hands. Anthropologist Clifford Geertz reminds us that this kind of understanding misses the most fascinating parts. He famously said, "Man is an animal suspended in webs of significance he himself has spun." This means no one lives simply in a pile of rigid customs ; everyone lives in meaning, and you must place a small action back into the actor’s own context to understand it. Therefore, he argues that studying culture is like decoding—you have to look past the surface; the difference.

is not in the act itself, but in the meaning behind it. He gave an interesting example: winking and blinking. Looking only at the muscle twitch, the two are identical, but one is a flirtatious signal, while the other is just a twitch—the difference lies in the lens of the observer. Take the Muslim headscarf as an example; placing it in different contexts makes it an entirely different thing. During the Algerian War of Independence, it was a tool of political resistance, with female fighters hiding weapons. beneath their veils. In French public schools, it is legally labeled as a religious symbol, turning it into a battlefield for secularism. In contemporary Indonesian cities, it blends with fashion trends to become an accessory for young women to express their style. And during the Eid al-Fitr celebrations at the Taipei Main Station lobby, it is a warm and lively symbol of festive gathering for migrant workers. Next time you feel uncomfortable observing the behavior of a different ethnic group, why not ask. yourself: is their life actually strange, or have the lenses in our eyes long been tinted a specific color? And who helped us tint them? Who exactly fitted these lenses for us? Actually, it’s a factory setting. You spend years wearing glasses with yellowish lenses, until one day you take them off to look at a white wall and realize, " Wow, the wall is actually this white!" But before taking them off, if someone came up and told you the wall was pure. white, you might think they were crazy, because in your field of vision, that pale yellow is simply the color a wall is supposed to be. If a ruler has been placed before our eyes since birth, how on earth are we supposed to notice it? Using one's own cultural habits to measure others, only to find them increasingly strange, is academically called ethnocentrism. What’s most intriguing isn't that this phenomenon is everywhere, but why this ruler seems so self-evident and natural. 19. th-century Europe gave a very arrogant answer, believing that all human cultures were climbing the same ladder, just at different speeds. Since there was only this single path for the whole world, European civilization, being at the front, felt perfectly justified in using its own standards as the benchmark. The father of modern anthropology, Boas, spent his life overturning this arrogant script. In " Race, Language, and Culture," he argued that every cultural group has its own. unique historical context, and it is impossible to force any nation’s experience onto a single evolutionary chart. In other words, there is no shared ladder in the world; every society follows its own path. This position is called "historical particularism." He shattered the prejudices of the 19th century. Boas pointed out that culture is infinitely complex, and there is no such thing as a universal law of evolution that applies everywhere. Once you admit there is no shared, hierarchical ladder. , using your own standards to rank others becomes completely indefensible. What is the difference between these two ways of thinking? For the most direct example: seeing a Muslim woman wearing a veil, those who think they are ahead will shake their heads and say, "That’s too backward, not yet enlightened." But Boas would hold you back and say, "Don't laugh; that is a meaning of life that grew out of their own history." So, just how overbearing is this ruler in reality? Take France’s 2004 school headscarf ban as.

an example. Officials spoke nicely, saying "discreet" religious symbols were allowed but "conspicuous" ones were not. The question is: what counts as conspicuous? A cross necklace tucked under a shirt is called "discreet," but a headscarf covering hair is called " too ostentatious." Who gets to make that call? The majority, of course. Ironically, the authorities claim they are protecting girls from tradition, yet if a girl speaks up to say her headscarf is her own choice, the system. simply assumes she’s been brainwashed . This is the most terrifying form of ethnocentrism; it’s never about shouting insults, but rather that arrogant certainty that "I'm doing this for your own good." Bringing the scene back to Taiwan, our schools were actually exactly the same. In the past, schools mandated short hair for all students in the name of "neatness." If a student couldn't cut their hair due to religion, parents had to write letters and go around bowing their heads to justify their "special" status . Standards are always set by the majority, leaving only the "different" individuals to sweat and struggle to explain to the whole world why they aren't "normal." Returning to those pale yellow glasses: we don't need to rush to deny our own biases. The first step is simply to admit them. The lenses in front of our eyes come with factory settings from birth. The biggest problem is that these glasses don't just color the world; they also flatten the people walking toward us into two-dimensional silhouettes. Ethnocentrism makes it harder to see the real person in front of us. When a. group of people is reduced to flat outlines in our eyes, how easily is their right to speak stripped away? Our brains are lazy and often imagine someone to be a completely different species from us, erasing their unique personalities and replacing them with rigid labels. In sociology, this is called "othering." In his classic work* Orientalism*, Edward Said argued that the West's massive theories depicting the East were never just sketches; they. were a means of establishing authority. The issue isn't whether the outsider's portrait is accurate, but rather who is holding the brush. This insight hits the blind spot: the point of criticism isn't to catch what was said wrong, but to recognize that the rules of this script are held by a select few. The people being depicted are forced to play bit parts in others 'stories forever; even if they want to rewrite the script, the microphone is never in their hands. Applying this logic back. to the Muslim headscarf: when mainstream society defines it as a symbol of female oppression, the women who wear it are left with only two roles: victims needing "civilized" salvation, or fanatics to be strictly guarded against. If they say "this is my own decision" or "this is my personal freedom," how will others perceive them? I think most people would say they've been brainwashed too deeply and haven't truly awakened; only when they weep and accuse others of persecution will everyone nod in. satisfaction and say, "See? I knew it." When a person is only allowed to be a victim or a fanatic, every word they say will be twisted into the script others want to hear. In 1958, the story of Algerian women being forced to burn their veils in public became headline news precisely because it perfectly fit the colonizer's narrative of the barbaric being saved by the civilized. Take a common trope in our news: when a migrant worker gets a certification or an award, the headline reads, "This foreign worker is different." Think.

carefully about that phrase—behind the praise lies the assumption that other migrant workers are supposed to be inferior and have no future. Right? On the surface, it’s praise; in reality, it treats them as a mere exception. If this award-winning worker tried to talk about labor conditions, overtime pay, or vacation rights in front of a microphone, these truly important voices would likely be wiped clean, because they don't fit the script. The cruelest harm of "othering" isn't how harshly people speak to you, but the way a preconceived framework strips you of the chance to defend yourself—but it doesn't end there. Have you all seen Dragon Ball? Characters wear green scouters to analyze power levels, but some levels can't be measured; you might think the device is glitchy, but the numbers are actually forced upon you. When these " power levels" are converted into government budgets, how should we evaluate them? Ranking civilizations. from high to low, distinguishing between the civilized and the barbaric, the progressive and the backward, and insisting the lower must emulate the higher—in academia, this is called cultural hierarchy. Once this hierarchy is established, it’s no longer just private grumbling; it becomes a roadmap guiding how power is exercised. The most famous example is political scientist Samuel Huntington, who asserted in "The Clash of Civilizations " that after the Cold War, the most serious human conflict would no longer be the ideological struggle between. capitalism and communism, but clashes between different civilizations. The world would be reshuffled along civilizational lines, making identity the most volatile battlefield. This theory exposes a reality: cultural differences are easily exploited by politicians for their own agendas. But as anthropologist Eric Wolf asked in " Europe and the People Without History," where on earth are there so many closed-off, unrelated civilizations? These civilizations, from beginning to end, were forged by humanity through. trade, conquest, and migration; civilization is the result of dynamic collisions. Looking back at the 1958 farce in Algeria where veils were publicly burned, it was the rawest official display of cultural intolerance: the French colonial government brought in troops, set up cameras, and staged a show of "savage women." The play portrayed them being saved and liberated by French civilization, packaging their colonial rule as noble enlightenment while branding local customs as symbols of backward decay. When intolerance. reaches this level, it is no longer just personal prejudice; it becomes a political act fueled by budgets, military mobilization, and carefully staged lenses. If prejudice stays in one's head, it doesn't cost a dime, but when it becomes policy, it drains massive budgets. That is why cultural intolerance is not merely a moral issue , but a genuine struggle for power. Take an example from daily life: a certain city holds a multicultural festival, with promotional materials filled with words like "inclusion" and. "respect," yet one look at the venue layout and schedule reveals the truth. Stalls for Southeast Asian migrant workers are shoved to the outermost perimeter, next to portable toilets and trash cans, with their performances relegated to a 20-minute slot at 3 PM in the scorching sun, while the main stage is generously handed over to expensive pop bands for a full hour. Promotional materials are never stupid enough to write who is superior or inferior, but the budget sheets and floor plans do, and the schedule allocations make it perfectly clear. Cultural intolerance is rarely printed.

in slogans; it usually lies quietly within government budgets. So, how do we address this issue systematically? Article 10, Paragraph 11 of the Additional Articles of the Constitution of the Republic of China explicitly affirms multiculturalism and forbids state power from leading cultural intolerance. Implemented in real life, the Taiwan Railways Administration later officially opened a Muslim prayer room on the basement floor of Taipei Main Station, equipped with a qibla and washing facilities, becoming a pioneer. among Taiwan's transport hubs. Let’s use another example: when the Algerian War of Independence broke out in November 1954, there was an object fiercely contested from the start—the white haik worn by women. In the urban warfare of Algiers, female members once used it to smuggle bombs. After the French military caught onto their inspection techniques, the women switched to European-style clothing to pass through. The French side judged that to dismantle the local society's structure of resistance, they must. first make the women take off their veils. Please note the logic behind this judgment: they were not discussing clothing; they were discussing tactics. A piece of cloth here is no longer just clothing; it is a strategic objective. On May 13, 1958, a power seizure occurred in Algiers, and on that very same day in the city center, a public unveiling ceremony was held, hosted by the wives of high-ranking garrison officers. Women stepped forward, declaring their desire to be liberated, removing their veils and burning them, shouting, "Like French women!" Cameras. circled the area while armed soldiers maintained order. A few days later, pro-French newspapers declared on their front pages that a large number of Muslim women had taken a stand. There is a set of figures here I hope you will remember: researchers estimate the actual number of participants was between a few dozen and a few hundred, while the newspaper claimed it was several thousand. If we shift the lens to the individual, the picture changes entirely. One woman who had never even worn a veil only attended because her. brother was in French custody; she was coerced into participating in exchange for his life. Thus, this exhibition of "voluntary liberation" was conditioned by duress, where the individual and the collective exposed each other. Viewed from above, it was an awakening with impressive statistics; viewed from below, it was a person's desperate calculation in an extreme situation. This is the cruelty of othering. Within that framework, her true situation could never be voiced, because the. framework only required her action, not her reasons. Now, let’s apply the five concepts mentioned today to this scene one by one. First is culture. The French were never just dealing with a piece of cloth, but with religious norms, structures, and social networks. Precisely because it was an integrated piece of a whole, the French judged that removing this one item could affect the entire situation. This judgment was tactically accurate, and that is exactly what made it so terrifying. Second is cultural difference; that same piece of cloth. meant completely different things within the two respective systems. For the French, it was proof of backwardness; for the local society, it was a part of daily life and a resource that could be used for resistance. The two sides weren't fighting over who owned the item, but over what it signified. Third is ethnocentrism. The French line of reasoning was: because our women don't wear it, not wearing it is progressive; and because not wearing it is progressive, taking it off is liberation. This logic never departed.

from its own measuring stick, yet they felt they were speaking about universal truths the entire time. Fourth is othering. Local women were predefined as a category in need of saving, so they only needed to appear and perform that act to complete the entire script. The fifth is cultural intervention. The previous four layers combined finally evolve into an action plan: selecting a date, clearing the site, and moving in. Bringing in the military, arranging the cameras, and issuing headlines—this is the complete form of intervention. It’s not just a statement, but an executable plan. Forty-six years later, the same set of "graduations"(lenses) changed location and methodology. On December 17, 2003, the French President delivered a speech advocating for an explicit ban on wearing symbols of overt religious affiliation in public primary and secondary schools. On March 3, 2004, the Senate passed the law to take effect that September, designating it as Article L 141-5-1 in the Education Code, while clarifying which religious symbols were permissible. In. this controversy, one side argues that campus should be a shared space where students are not segregated by religious affiliation, while the other side notes this line practically falls on Muslim female students, and under the name of protection, strips them of the chance to explain their reasons. The biggest difference from 1958 is the means: 1958 used the military and cameras, while 2004 used legislative procedures, committee reports, and code articles. The means shifted from. coercion to legality, the setting from a colony to the home country, and the justification from liberation to secularism. Yet one thing remains unchanged: the person deciding what that piece of cloth means is still not the person wearing it. The 1958 lens perceived the veil as backward, while the 2004 lens perceived it as insufficiently secular. The name of the lens has changed, but the lens itself remains. The one thing we shouldn't do with this example is use it to cast blame, because both eras believed they were helping. In both cases, someone. else substituted the wearer to decide what that piece of cloth meant. Any society, while acting under the assumption of good intentions, might use its own ruler to measure everyone else. When you discover our cultures are different, what should we do? In reality, the filter cannot be taken off ; anyone viewing the world must do so through some language, some set of customs, and some span of history. This is not a defect; this is precisely the result of having a culture. So, if. someone tells you, "I am completely objective and have no stance," that statement itself is a pair of very thick, prescribed glasses. What we can actually do are three things: first, know that you are wearing them; second, recognize who etched the graduations onto those lenses. Third, before passing judgment on others' lives, let them first explain what that thing means within their own system. These three things aren't romantic, but they are all things that can be practiced.
